title: Sorting the sky in 30 seconds
teaches: How high is that cloud, just by looking? The three floors, how cloud names work, and three quick tricks: edges, the outstretched hand and shaded bellies. Meet altocumulus, cirrocumulus and cirrus

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: The weather has three floors: **low**, from the ground to about 2 km (6,500 feet); **middle**, about 2 to 7 km (6,500 to 23,000 feet); and **high**, from about 5 km (16,500 feet) to the top of the weather. Temperature, and so what a cloud is made of, is what really sets them apart.
Trick 1, **edges**: droplet clouds have crisp edges and live low; ice clouds have soft, silky, feathery edges and live high. The purest ice cloud is **cirrus**.
The names are a code: *cumulus* a heap, *stratus* a layer, *cirrus* a curl of hair, *nimbus* rain-bearing; *cirro-* puts a cloud on the high floor, *alto-* on the middle.

Trick 2, **the hand**: at arm’s length, lumps wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, from a little-finger nail to three fingers are **altocumulus**, and grains smaller than a nail are **cirrocumulus**.
Trick 3, **shaded bellies**: altocumulus lumps have grey undersides; cirrocumulus grains are pure white.

blocks.text: The first two lessons showed how heaps and sheets form, and which of them rain. This one sorts them by height, like the floors of a building, and gives you three tricks for doing it in half a minute with nothing but your eyes and your hand.

Almost all weather happens in the lowest ten or twelve kilometres of the atmosphere, and meteorologists divide that space into three floors. The **low** floor runs from the ground up to about 2,000 metres (6,500 feet). The **middle** floor runs from 2,000 to about 7,000 metres (23,000 feet). The **high** floor starts around 5,000 metres (16,500 feet), overlapping the middle one, and reaches up to the top of the weather at ten or twelve kilometres. Those heights are only guidelines, and the middle and high floors overlap because what really gives a cloud its character is the temperature where it forms, which shifts from day to day and from summer to winter. A cloud at six kilometres could belong to either the middle or the high floor; you tell which one by what the cloud is made of and how it looks.

Whereas a rising dry bubble always cools at 10 °C per kilometre, the surrounding sky has its own temperature profile shaped by ground heating, sunlight, wind stirring and large-scale sinking. On an average day the surrounding air gets colder by about 6.5 °C for every kilometre you climb (about 3.6 °F per 1,000 feet).

If the valley starts at a mild 15 °C, the surrounding air hits freezing (0 °C) a little over two kilometres up, and drops to around −40 °C by nine kilometres. Below freezing, cloud water can freeze into ice, so altitude and temperature determine what a cloud is made of, which in turn determines how it looks. (In the figure, you will notice that cloud droplets often stay liquid well below 0 °C; Lesson 7 explores why.)

blocks.caption: A mild summer day, from the valley floor to the top of the weather.

blocks.text: Low clouds consist almost entirely of liquid water droplets packed closely together, often hundreds of them in every cubic centimetre. At the outer edge of a liquid cloud, where it mixes with drier air, those tiny droplets evaporate in seconds, giving low clouds crisp, sharp outlines.

Higher up in the sky, more of the cloud water freezes into ice crystals. Ice crystals are much larger than droplets, far fewer in number, and spaced much further apart. In addition, the cold air surrounding high clouds already contains nearly all the water vapour that ice can sustain, so a crystal drifting out into clear air sublimates (turns straight back into vapour) very slowly. Instead of vanishing in seconds, ice crystals linger for minutes and trail out in long streamers across the sky. As a result, high clouds look thin, silky, and fibrous, with feathery edges. Simply looking at whether a cloud’s edges are *sharp* or *feathery* will usually tell you which floor it belongs to.

blocks.caption: The edge of a cloud, magnified.

blocks.text: The purest cloud of the high floor is **cirrus**: detached white wisps, threads and hooks, made entirely of ice crystals trailing out in the wind. Its edges are the softest in the sky, so it is the easiest cloud of all to put on its floor. What its hooks and its spreading say about tomorrow is the next lesson.

blocks.caption: Some of today’s sky.
blocks.task: File each cloud onto its floor.

blocks.text: One cloud refuses to stay on a single floor. A full-grown thunderstorm tower, or cumulonimbus, starts on the low floor and punches all the way to the top of the weather (the troposphere, the layer of air we live in). It gets a category of its own, which Lesson 5 covers.
Cloud names can sound like Latin incantations at first, but they follow a simple naming system, and you already know half the pieces.

In 1802, an amateur meteorologist in London named Luke Howard classified clouds using Latin roots, and nearly every cloud name used today combines four of his original words with a fifth added later in the century. **Cumulus** means a heap and **stratus** means a layer, the two basic textures from Lesson 1. **Cirrus** means a curl of hair, describing the wispy ice clouds of the high floor. **Nimbus** means a rain-bearing cloud. The fifth root, **alto**, was added later in the 1800s. Although *alto* literally means high in Latin, *cirrus* was already established for the highest floor, so *alto-* was assigned to the middle floor just below it.

To name a cloud, you combine its floor prefix with its texture. The prefix *cirro-* (from cirrus) places a cloud on the high floor, *alto-* places it on the middle floor, and low-floor clouds take no height prefix at all. A flat layer on the middle floor is therefore an altostratus, while small heaps on the high floor are cirrocumulus.

blocks.caption: The sky, one name at a time.
blocks.task: Build each name from its height and texture.

targets.clue: Rounded heaps in rows on the middle floor
A grey sheet over the sun on the middle floor
A thin, even veil on the high floor

blocks.caption: Three floors and two textures make six names.

blocks.text: Combining floors and textures gives six of the ten main cloud types (or genera). The remaining four modify the pattern slightly. **Cirrus** on its own refers to detached high-altitude curls and wisps. **Stratocumulus** describes low heaps that have merged into a lumpy layer. **Nimbostratus** is a deep, rain-bearing layer, and **cumulonimbus** is a towering, rain-bearing heap. That makes ten main cloud types in total, all catalogued and photographed in the World Meteorological Organization’s **International Cloud Atlas**, the standard field guide used by weather services around the world.

The middle floor runs from about two to seven kilometres up, where the air is near or below freezing and clouds usually consist of a mixture of liquid droplets and ice crystals. On most days, thermals rising from the sun-warmed ground never reach this high; the atmosphere above a kilometre or two is stable, so rising bubbles lose their buoyancy on the low floor where fair-weather cumulus clouds flatten out. (On days with deep instability, storm towers punch through every floor, as Lesson 5 shows.)

Middle-floor clouds usually form a different way: a wide layer of moist air glides slowly upward over hundreds of kilometres, most often out ahead of a storm, which the next lesson follows. Lifting a whole layer gently makes a sheet, just as on the low floor.

A cloud sheet on the middle floor does not always stay smooth, however. Just as the ground cools at night by radiating infrared light out to space, clouds radiate infrared energy too. The top of a cloud layer radiates infrared heat straight up into the cold, clear sky above and receives very little radiation back, so the top of the cloud cools steadily. Meanwhile, the base of the cloud faces the warmer ground below, absorbing roughly as much infrared heat from the earth as it radiates downward. During the day, sunlight warms the cloud top slightly, but because white cloud droplets reflect most incoming sunlight, infrared cooling still dominates for most of the day and night. As a result, the top of the cloud layer grows progressively colder than its base.

Inside a cloud, a parcel of air moving up or down changes temperature by only about 5 °C per kilometre, because condensing water releases heat and evaporating water soaks it up (latent heat, which Lesson 5 puts to work). Once radiative cooling makes the top of the cloud layer more than 5 °C per kilometre colder than the base, the layer becomes unstable within itself. A pocket of chilled, dense air at the top sinks and stays colder than the cloudy air around it, while warmer air from the base rises to take its place. The layer begins to overturn in regular convection cells, each forming a loop with rising air in one place and sinking air right beside it.

Loops that are much wider than they are tall have to drag air a long way horizontally, while loops that are very narrow experience too much friction against their neighbours, so the cells naturally settle into roughly equal width and height, about as wide as the cloud layer is deep (typically a few hundred metres). Where air rises in each cell, the cloud thickens into a rounded lump; where air sinks, the droplets evaporate and the cloud thins or clears. In this way, a smooth cloud sheet breaks up into a pattern of rounded patches or rolls. (The same cooling at the cloud top also helps keep stratocumulus decks on the low floor stirred and broken into lumps, along with the heating from below.)

blocks.caption: A cloud layer cooled from the top, turning over in cells.

blocks.text: So every floor has its lumpy layer. Low, it is **stratocumulus**, from the last lesson. On the middle floor it is **altocumulus**: rounded patches or rolls separated by lanes of clear sky, often compared to a flock of sheep. And on the high floor it is **cirrocumulus**: tiny white grains or ripples in regular rows like fish scales, a pattern sailors called a *mackerel sky*. Cirrocumulus is usually short-lived, because the supercooled droplets that help start the ripples soon freeze into cirrus.

At first glance, a layer of altocumulus looks very similar to **stratocumulus** on the low floor or **cirrocumulus** on the high floor. All three consist of patches or rolls arranged in a layer, and from the ground there are no landmarks in the sky to judge their altitude against. How can you tell which floor the layer is on?

You can judge their height by the apparent size of the individual cloud elements. Because overturning cells are roughly as wide as their cloud layer is deep, low and middle cloud layers (both typically a few hundred metres thick) break into lumps that are a few hundred metres across. High-floor cloud layers are much shallower, often less than a hundred metres thick, so cirrocumulus ripples are physically smaller as well as much further away. Just as a car looks smaller in the distance, the higher a cloud layer sits, the smaller its individual lumps *look* from the ground.

In the figure, which views the sky high up where you would normally measure, a 300-metre lump at an altitude of 2 km spans an **angle** of about 7° across your field of view; at 5 km up it spans about 3°, and a 100-metre grain at 9 km spans less than 1°.

You always carry a reliable ruler for measuring angles: your own hand held at arm’s length. With your arm stretched out straight, a closed fist covers about 10° of sky, three fingers side by side cover about 5°, a thumb covers about 2°, and the nail of your little finger covers about 1°. Because people with larger hands also have proportionally longer arms that hold the hand further from the eye, the geometry cancels out and these angles hold true for almost everyone.

blocks.caption: A layer of lumpy cloud, seen from the ground with your arm stretched out.
blocks.task: Move the layer through the three floors and see each verdict.

blocks.text: This gives a practical rule of thumb with your arm fully extended: cloud elements **wider than three fingers** are stratocumulus, elements between a **little-finger nail and three fingers** (roughly the width of a thumb) are altocumulus, and elements **smaller than your little-finger nail** are cirrocumulus. Always measure clouds high up in the sky, well away from the horizon. Near the horizon, you are looking at clouds that are much further away and viewing them obliquely from the side, which makes every element appear foreshortened and deceptively small.

Shading provides a second clue to a cloud’s floor. When sunlight enters the top of a cloud, the water droplets scatter the light in all directions, bouncing much of it right back out the top. The deeper light travels into the cloud, the less of it remains to emerge from the bottom. A very thin cloud lets most of the sunlight pass through and looks uniformly white from underneath. A cloud lump several hundred metres thick, on the other hand, reflects most of the sunlight back into space and lets much less reach its base, so from the ground you see a shaded underside: grey in the centre with bright white edges where sunlight catches the thinner sides. (The base looks grey rather than pitch black because some diffused sunlight still filters through from above, while the ground and surrounding sky reflect light upward from below.)

blocks.caption: One lump of cloud with the sun above it.
blocks.task: Thicken the cloud until it shades itself.

blocks.text: Altocumulus elements are usually deep enough to show **shaded bellies**, looking like grey-bottomed sheep in a flock. Cirrocumulus, being thin and composed of ice crystals high aloft, consists of pure white grains with **no shading at all**. Checking for shading quickly distinguishes altocumulus from cirrocumulus, while the hand test distinguishes altocumulus from lower, larger stratocumulus.

parts.title: The sky, or a photo of it

blocks.text: One warning before the check. Your hand measures **angles in the real sky**, not on a screen. A photograph can be zoomed in or out, and printed or shown at any size, so the same lumps can fill a picture or shrink to grains in it. Holding your hand up to a photo tells you nothing.

To put a cloud in a photograph on its floor, use the clues inside the picture itself. **Edges**: crisp or feathery. **Bellies**: grey, shaded undersides or pure white grains. **The sun**, if it is in the shot, is half a degree across, about half a little-finger nail at arm’s length: lumps several suns wide are low or middle, grains smaller than the sun are high. And **the ground**: a tree, a barn, a ridge or a grain elevator gives the picture its scale, and low cloud often sits close above them or hides the hilltops.

blocks.title: Sorting the sky in thirty seconds
points: Edges first: crisp means droplets and low or middle; soft and feathery means ice and high.
Lumps in a layer? Hold your hand out, high in the sky: wider than three fingers is stratocumulus, a nail to three fingers altocumulus, smaller than a nail cirrocumulus.
Check the bellies: grey shading rules out cirrocumulus.
In a photo, use edges, bellies, the size of the sun and the ground, never your hand.

blocks.text: For each photo, decide which floor the cloud belongs to: low, middle, or high. For cumulus heaps, report the floor where the base sits. These are photographs, so your hand won’t help: on lumpy layers look for shaded bellies and compare the lumps with the sun or the ground; on wisps and streaks, look at the edges.

blocks.caption: Real photos. Which floor is each cloud on?
The sky right now. Which floor, and what is it?

items.question: High overhead is a layer of rounded lumps with grey bellies. At arm’s length, each lump is about as wide as your thumb. Which floor is it on?
options: Low floor: stratocumulus, because grey bellies mean thick, low cloud
Middle floor: altocumulus, a thumb wide and shaded underneath
High floor: cirrocumulus, because the lumps look small and far off
items.why: Measured high in the sky, lumps between a little-finger nail and three fingers wide are altocumulus. The shaded bellies rule out the thin, pure white grains of cirrocumulus.

items.question: White threads and hooks with soft, silky edges trail across a blue sky, with no lumps and no shading at all. Which floor are they on?
options: High floor: cirrus, because soft, feathery edges mean ice
Low floor: wisps of stratus left over from the morning fog
Middle floor: altocumulus pulled into threads by the wind
items.why: Feathery, fibrous edges are ice crystals that linger as they evaporate. Droplet clouds evaporate in seconds and keep crisp outlines. Detached ice wisps are cirrus, on the high floor.

items.question: A patch of tiny white ripples in rows, each smaller than your little-finger nail at arm’s length, with no grey underneath. What is it?
options: Altocumulus: a flock of sheep seen from very far away
Stratocumulus: a low sheet thinning out as it breaks up
Cirrocumulus: high grains too thin to shade themselves
items.why: Grains smaller than a nail, measured high in the sky, are cirrocumulus, and their pure white undersides confirm it: a layer that thin cannot shade itself.

items.question: In a photograph, a layer of lumps fills the frame. Held up to the screen, each lump is a little-finger nail wide, but the lumps are grey underneath and almost touch a grain elevator. Which floor?
options: High floor: the hand test on the screen says cirrocumulus
Low floor: the grey bellies and the elevator give it away
No way to tell from a photograph without a measured sun
items.why: A photo can be zoomed to any size, so the hand test means nothing on a screen. Clues in the picture do: grey shaded bellies and a cloud base just over a building put it low, as stratocumulus.

learned: The weather has three floors: low (ground to about 2 km, 6,500 feet), middle (about 2 to 7 km) and high (about 5 km to the top of the weather). Temperature, rather than exact altitude, is what truly separates them.
Low clouds are closely packed droplets with crisp edges; high clouds are ice crystals that evaporate slowly, giving soft, fibrous, feathery edges. Detached ice wisps are cirrus.

Cloud names combine roots and height prefixes: cumulus (heap), stratus (layer), cirrus (curl of hair) and nimbus (rain-bearing); cirro- marks the high floor, alto- the middle, and low clouds take no prefix.
A cloud layer cooled at its top overturns into lumps: stratocumulus low, altocumulus in the middle, cirrocumulus high.

Held at arm’s length, a fist spans about 10° of sky, three fingers 5°, a thumb 2° and a little-finger nail 1°. High in the sky, lumps wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, a nail to three fingers altocumulus, smaller than a nail cirrocumulus.
Altocumulus lumps have grey, shaded bellies; cirrocumulus grains are pure white. In a photograph, judge floors by edges, bellies, the size of the sun and the ground, not by your hand.

floors.title: The three floors
floors.text: Low floor: ground to about 2,000 m, composed of liquid water droplets with sharp edges. Middle floor: about 2,000 to 7,000 m, composed of liquid droplets and some ice. High floor: above about 5,000 m, composed of ice crystals with thin, silky, fibrous edges. Because the atmosphere cools by about 6.5 °C per kilometre on average, these floors correspond to temperature zones. Towering cumulonimbus clouds span all three floors.

roots.title: Name roots
roots.text: Cumulus means a heap, stratus a flat layer, cirrus a curl of hair, and nimbus a rain-bearing cloud. The prefix cirro- places a cloud on the high floor and alto- places it on the middle floor, while low-floor clouds take no prefix. Together these roots form the ten main cloud genera.

hand-trick.title: The hand trick
hand-trick.text: With your arm stretched out straight, a closed fist covers about 10° of sky, three fingers 5°, a thumb 2°, and a little-finger nail 1°. Because higher cloud layers are further away, their individual lumps look smaller: elements wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, elements between a nail and three fingers are altocumulus, and grains smaller than a nail are cirrocumulus. Grey, shaded undersides indicate a thicker layer of droplets (stratocumulus or altocumulus, never cirrocumulus). The trick works on the real sky only: a photograph can be zoomed to any size.

altocumulus.title: Altocumulus
altocumulus.text: Rounded patches or rolls with grey, shaded bellies on the middle floor, spanning between a little-finger nail and three fingers at arm’s length. They form when a middle-level cloud sheet cools at its top by radiating infrared energy and overturns into convection cells. Morning turrets (castellanus) indicate middle-level instability and warn of afternoon thunderstorms.

cirrocumulus.title: Cirrocumulus
cirrocumulus.text: A thin high-altitude layer of tiny white grains or ripples without grey shading (a mackerel sky), where each element is smaller than a little-finger nail held at arm’s length. Cirrocumulus patches are brief and transitional, sometimes appearing ahead of an approaching weather system.
